# Noninfectious tenosynovitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Noninfectious tenosynovitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/3Q0SDf)

---

## Summary

Noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u> is inflammation or thickening of a <u>tendon</u> and/or its synovial sheath due to repetitive use injury or <u>chronic inflammation</u> from systemic disease. It typically presents with <u>pain</u> and swelling across the affected <u>tendon</u>. Noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u> commonly affects the hands (e.g., <u>trigger digit</u>, <u>De Quervain tenosynovitis</u>), but can also occur in other <u>tendons</u> throughout the body. Diagnosis is clinical. Diagnostic studies and imaging are reserved for suspected underlying systemic disease or diagnostic uncertainty. Initial treatment is conservative and includes <u>glucocorticoid</u> injection, splinting, <u>physical therapy</u>, <u>occupational therapy</u>, and oral <u>NSAIDs</u>. Surgical release is typically reserved for severe or refractory symptoms.




See also “<u>Infectious tenosynovitis</u>” and “<u>Insertional tendinopathy</u>”.

---

## Etiology

* Repetitive use of the involved <u>tendon</u> [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)

* Systemic disease (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>gout</u>, <u>thyroid disease</u>) [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)

---

## Clinical features

Clinical features differ depending on which <u>tendons</u> are involved. See “<u>Trigger finger</u>” and “<u>de Quervain tenosynovitis</u>” for clinical features specific to those conditions. [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)[[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)




* <u>Pain</u> along the affected <u>tendon</u> that worsens with movement and typically improves with rest

* Swelling

* Tenderness, <u>nodules</u>, and/or <u>crepitus</u> upon palpation

* Decreased <u>range of motion</u>





> [!WARNING]
> The presence of <u>clinical features of infectious tenosynovitis</u> is a <u>medical emergency</u>.

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Trigger finger [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)[[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* The most common <u>tendon</u> pathology, affecting

* ∼ 2% of the general population [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)

* ∼ 20% of individuals with <u>diabetes</u> [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (∼ 6:1) [[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)

* <u>Incidence</u> highest in children < 8 years old and adults 40–60 years old [[4]](/library/6zWjFL0)





#### Pathophysiology




<u>Fibrocartilaginous</u> <u>metaplasia</u> of the <u>tendon sheath</u> of the A1 annular pulley  → loss of smooth gliding of the finger flexor <u>tendons</u> under the annular pulley → finger catching or becoming locked in a flexed position




#### Clinical features




* Most often affects the ring finger or thumb [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)

* <u>Pain</u>, tenderness, and/or palpable <u>nodule</u> at the <u>palmar</u> base of the affected finger

* Palpable <u>crepitus</u> with movement

* Catching or locking in a flexed position with painful popping on <u>flexion</u> or extension

* Often concurrent with <u>carpal tunnel syndrome</u>  [[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)





> [!TIP]
> Individuals with <u>diabetes</u> often have involvement of multiple fingers. [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)




#### Management




See “<u>Diagnostics of noninfectious tenosynovitis</u>” and “Treatment of noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u>.”




### De Quervain tenosynovitis [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)[[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (∼ 3:1) [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)

* Age of onset: 40–59 years [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)

* More common in

* Golfers, tennis players [[5]](/library/0Tde660)

* Individuals who frequently text or play video games

* Caregivers for <u>infants</u> or pets (“mother's thumb”)

* Pregnant, postpartum, and lactating individuals

* Individuals with <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u> [[6]](/library/dTdop60)





#### Pathophysiology




Repetitive and/or prolonged <u>abduction</u> and extension of the thumb → noninflammatory thickening (i.e., myxoid degeneration and <u>fibrosis</u>) of the <u>abductor pollicis longus</u> and <u>extensor pollicis brevis</u> <u>tendons</u>




![De Quervain tenosynovitis](media/dt0eg4m1jd70l6idhdsd2g4u.jpg)

De Quervain tenosynovitis




#### Clinical features [[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)




* <u>Pain</u> and/or swelling of the dorsoradial wrist and base of the thumb overlying the <u>radial styloid</u>

* <u>Pain</u> exacerbated by movement of the thumb and/or wrist (e.g., when grasping objects)

* <u>Pain</u> may radiate proximally to forearm





#### Diagnostics




* Diagnosis is clinical.

* A positive Finkelstein test on examination supports the diagnosis. ;  [[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)[[7]](/library/-XdD0K0)

* Description: The examiner grasps the thumb of the affected hand and exerts longitudinal <u>traction</u>, passively pulling the thumb across the palm to cause <u>ulnar deviation</u> of the wrist.

* Test is positive if <u>pain</u> or discomfort is elicited over the dorsoradial wrist (very high <u>specificity</u>) [[7]](/library/-XdD0K0)

* See also “<u>Diagnostics of noninfectious tenosynovitis</u>.”





![Finkelstein test](media/zsua5liz8uyuluu5ry0kw5v8.jpg)

Finkelstein test




#### Treatment




See “Treatment of noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u>.”

---

## Diagnosis

* Noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.

* If concern for underlying systemic disease or diagnostic uncertainty, consider:

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> as indicated (e.g., <u>serological testing in rheumatoid arthritis</u>)

* Imaging [[8]](/library/2cdTbK0)

* <u>X-ray</u>: recommended initial evaluation for chronic symptoms in patients with hand or wrist involvement

* <u>MRI</u> or <u>ultrasound</u>: can be used to evaluate the <u>tendon</u> and <u>synovium</u>





> [!TIP]
> Diagnostic studies are not usually necessary for the diagnosis of noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u>. [[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)

---

## Treatment

Initial management of noninfectious <u>tenosynovitis</u> is conservative. Refer patients with severe or refractory symptoms for surgical evaluation.




### <u>Conservative management</u> [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)[[9]](/library/m-WVBL0)




* <u>Glucocorticoid</u> injection into the affected <u>tendon sheath</u> (may be performed under US guidance) [[10]](/library/cTdap60)

* Effective in up to 90% of patients with <u>trigger finger</u> and ∼ 80% of patients with <u>De Quervain tenosynovitis</u> [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[2]](/library/z-Wr-L0)

* Repeat doses may be necessary.  [[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)

* Adverse effects include <u>atrophy</u> of <u>subcutaneous fat</u> and <u>tendon</u> degradation.

* Splinting (<u>immobilization</u>) of the affected area

* <u>Trigger finger</u>: <u>MCP</u> extension (preferred) or <u>DIP</u> extension <u>splint</u> for 4–6 weeks [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)

* <u>De Quervain tenosynovitis</u>: <u>thumb spica splint</u> for 3–4 weeks [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[9]](/library/m-WVBL0)

* Occupational and/or <u>physical therapy</u> (e.g., hand therapy) [[10]](/library/cTdap60)

* Oral <u>NSAIDs</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Glucocorticoid</u> injection should be offered as an initial treatment for most patients. [[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)[[9]](/library/m-WVBL0)[[11]](/library/dcdoYK0)




### <u>Surgery</u> [[1]](/library/pzWLFL0)[[3]](/library/YcdnaK0)[[9]](/library/m-WVBL0)




* Indications [[4]](/library/6zWjFL0)

* Severe symptoms

* Refractory symptoms despite 6 weeks of <u>conservative management</u>

* <u>Trigger digit</u> in individuals with <u>diabetes</u>

* Methods: usually involve release of the affected compartment, e.g.,

* <u>Trigger finger</u>: release of the A1 annular pulley of the affected finger

* <u>De Quervain tenosynovitis</u>: release of retinaculum of the first <u>dorsal</u> (extensor) compartment
